title: The counts are the best table
objectives: Derive that normalised counts maximise the likelihood of a bigram model, and smooth the zero counts.

screens.question: Which row gives these 272 pairs the higher likelihood?

options.text: Row B, the shares of the counts

options.why: You rewarded the row for being sure of u. It pays $-\ln 0.04$ on each of the 28 endings.

options.text: They tie, since both favour u
options.why: Both favour u, but the likelihood weighs every pair; the 66 that are not u decide it.

hints.text: The likelihood multiplies the chance of every one of the 272 pairs.
Compare $\sum_b N_b \ln q_b$: Row B gives $-237.43$, Row A $-260.49$.

feedback.correct: Row B: its log-likelihood is $-237.43$ against $-260.49$ for Row A.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Weigh each chance by how often its pair occurs.

byKey.A: You picked the surer row. Its 0.04 for the end costs $28 \times 3.22$ nats on the endings alone.

explain.text: The log-likelihood is $\sum_b N_b \ln q_b$: $-237.43$ for Row B and $-260.49$ for Row A. Row A gains on the 206 u’s but loses more on the 66 others. Row B is the counts divided by 272.

screens.title: Slide the chance of u
screens.prose: Move the chance of u. The other four share what is left in proportion to their counts. The caption gives the log-likelihood of the 272 pairs.
screens.question: At what chance of u is the log-likelihood largest? Give a decimal to 2 places.

hints.text: Watch the caption rise and then fall.

feedback.correct: About 0.76: the peak is at $206/272 = 0.757$, the share of u.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Slide slowly and find where the caption is least negative.

screens.title: The maximum likelihood row
screens.prose: The best chance for u was its share of the row. Name it: the **maximum likelihood estimate** of a row is its normalised counts, $\hat p_{ab} = N_{ab} / N_a$, where $N_a$ is the row’s total. A bigram row is a 27-sided coin.
screens.question: What is $\hat p$ for q then end? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: $28 / 272 = 0.1029$: about one q in ten ends a name.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the count by its row’s total.

byKey.whole-table: You divided by all 228,146 pairs. The chance after q divides by the 272 pairs after q.

explain.text: The row after q has 272 pairs, 28 of them into the end mark, so $\hat p = 28/272 = 0.1029$. Every cell of a row is its count over that row’s total.

screens.title: Why the shares win
screens.prose: Prove it for any row $a$ with $N_a > 0$, using the cross-entropy and KL facts from info level 2. Put the lines in order and leave out the one that does not belong.
screens.question: Put the steps in order.

lines.text: Each of the $N_{ab}$ pairs $a \to b$ has chance $q_b$, so the row’s log-likelihood is $\ell(q) = \sum_b N_{ab} \ln q_b$ (logs of a product add).
Write $\hat p_b = N_{ab}/N_a$, the row’s shares: $\ell(q) = N_a \sum_b \hat p_b \ln q_b$.
That sum is minus a cross-entropy (info l5): $\ell(q) = -N_a\, H(\hat p, q)$, in nats.
Split it (info l8): $H(\hat p, q) = H(\hat p) + D(\hat p \,\|\, q)$, and $H(\hat p)$ does not depend on $q$.
By Jensen (info l6), $D(\hat p \,\|\, q) \ge 0$, with equality only when $q = \hat p$.
Since $N_a > 0$, $\ell(q)$ is largest exactly when $q = \hat p$: the normalised counts.
Set $\partial \ell / \partial q_b = N_{ab}/q_b = 0$ for each $b$ on its own.
lines.why: The chances must add to 1, so they cannot move one at a time; and $N_{ab}/q_b$ is never 0 for a seen pair. The KL route needs no such step.

hints.text: Start from the likelihood of the row’s pairs.
Likelihood, shares, cross-entropy, split, KL at least 0, conclusion.

feedback.correct: The row’s log-likelihood is $-N_a H(\hat p, q)$, so it peaks where the KL term is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each line uses the one before it.

byKey.x1: Setting each derivative to 0 alone ignores that the chances add to 1. The KL route needs no constraint at all.

explain.text: The row’s log-likelihood is $-N_a$ times $H(\hat p, q) = H(\hat p) + D(\hat p \| q)$. Only the KL term depends on $q$, and it is 0 only at $q = \hat p$. So the counts over their row total are the maximum likelihood estimate.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide by row a’s total, 33,885.

screens.title: The coin inside the row
screens.prose: In estimation you found that a coin’s maximum likelihood chance of heads is the share of heads. Lump row a into two outcomes: the name ends, or a letter follows.

state.caption: Row a of $N$: 33,885 pairs in all.

screens.question: What is the maximum likelihood chance that a name ends straight after an a? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Treat the 33,885 a’s as 33,885 tosses.

byKey.per-name: You divided by the 32,033 names. Each a is one toss, so divide by the 33,885 a’s.

explain.text: With two outcomes the row is a coin tossed 33,885 times, landing “end” 6,640 times. Its MLE is the share, $0.1960$, the same as normalising the row.

screens.title: Smoothing
screens.prose: A zero count gives chance 0, and one unseen pair then makes a name impossible. **Smoothing** adds $\alpha$ to every count before normalising: $q_{ab} = (N_{ab} + \alpha)/(N_a + 27\alpha)$.
screens.question: With $\alpha = 1$, what is the chance of q then b, a pair the names never show? Give a decimal to 5 places.

hints.text: Every one of the 27 cells in the row gains 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The row total grows by 27, one for each cell.

byKey.one-cell: You added 1 to the row total once. All 27 cells gain 1, so the total grows by 27.
byKey.no-denominator: You left the row total at 272. The added counts belong in the total too.

explain.text: Adding 1 to all 27 cells makes the row total $272 + 27 = 299$, so the unseen pair gets $1/299 = 0.00334$. The rows still add to 1.

screens.title: How much to add
screens.prose: We shuffle the names with a fixed seed, count from 25,626 of them (the **training names**) and measure the loss on 3,203 others (the **dev names**). l3 explains the loss; lower is better.
screens.question: Which $\alpha$ would you keep?

options.why: Too little smoothing leaves unseen pairs nearly impossible: the dev loss is 2.4520.

options.text: 100: it protects every unseen pair most
options.why: So much smoothing flattens every row toward equal chances: the dev loss is 2.5507.
With no smoothing the dev loss is infinite: 7 dev pairs never occur in the training names.

feedback.correct: 0.1 or 1: both give 2.4514 on the dev names.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick the bar with the least dev loss.

byKey.none: The MLE is best on the names it was counted from. On new names a zero count is fatal.

explain.text: 0.1 and 1 tie at 2.4514 to four places, the least dev loss. Less smoothing leaves rare pairs too costly; more flattens the rows. The choice is made on dev names, never on the names counted.

screens.title: Divide by what?
screens.prose: To turn row n into chances, a learner divides each of its counts by 228,146, the table’s total. Row n holds 18,327 pairs.
screens.question: What do that learner’s chances in row n add up to? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the counts first, then divide by 228,146.

byKey.one: You assumed any division gives chances that add to 1. Only the row’s own total does that.

explain.text: Dividing by the table total gives $P(a, b)$, the chance of the pair, not $P(b \mid a)$. Row n then adds to $0.0803$, the share of pairs that start with n. Divide by the row’s own total, 18,327.

screens.title: Unseen on the dev names
screens.prose: With no smoothing, counts from the training names give 7 pairs of the dev names chance 0. They are z then v twice (tzvi and zvi), and g f, m f, x m, h h and m k (siegfried, comfort, maxmilian, noahh, omkar).
screens.question: What is the average loss on the dev names with no smoothing?

options.why: Add-one gave 2.4514 because no chance was 0. Without it, 7 chances are 0.

options.text: A little above 2.4514, from 7 pairs in 22,807
options.why: You let the 7 pairs cost a lot but not everything. A chance of 0 costs $-\ln 0 = \infty$.

hints.text: One infinite term makes the average infinite.

feedback.correct: Infinite: the 7 names are impossible under the unsmoothed table.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out the cost of one pair with chance 0.

byKey.skip: However rare, a pair with chance 0 costs $-\ln 0$, which is infinite, and so is the average.

explain.text: A pair with chance 0 costs $-\ln 0 = \infty$, so the dev average is infinite. Add-one gives each unseen pair a small chance, and the dev loss becomes 2.4514.

screens.title: bigram_probs() and nll() in code
screens.prose: Write `bigram_probs(N, alpha)`: add `alpha` to every count, then divide each row by its own total. Write `nll(P, words)`: the average of $-\ln P_{ab}$ over every pair of the words, marks included, using `index`. If a pair has chance 0, return `math.inf` (`math.log(0)` raises an error).
screens.question: Write `bigram_probs` and `nll`.

widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests: a planted 3 by 3 table with alpha 0 and 1, and the rows of the training table summing to 1 within 1e-12. Then come the dev loss with add-one counts from the training names (to 4 places), an unseen pair (`nll` must return `math.inf`), and equal chances on a short list. `train`, `dev`, `index`, `counts` and `N_train` are ready.
widget.prelude:
import math
import numpy as np

words = open('names.txt').read().splitlines()
perm = np.random.default_rng(42).permutation(len(words))
train = [words[i] for i in perm[:25626]]
dev = [words[i] for i in perm[25626:28829]]
index = {c: i + 1 for i, c in enumerate("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz")}
index["."] = 0


def counts(ws):
    N = np.zeros((27, 27), dtype=int)
    for w in ws:
        cs = "." + w + "."
        for a, b in zip(cs, cs[1:]):
            N[index[a], index[b]] += 1
    return N


N_train = counts(train)

In `nll`, return `math.inf` as soon as a pair has chance 0; otherwise divide the total by the number of pairs.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Each row must add to 1: divide by the row’s total, not the table’s.
byKey.test-5: tzvi holds z then v, unseen in the training names. Return `math.inf` for it.

explain.text: `bigram_probs` adds `alpha` and divides each row by its own total, so every row adds to 1. `nll` averages $-\ln P_{ab}$ over the pairs and is infinite if any chance is 0.

screens.title: Down after two down days
screens.prose: A desk wants the chance of a down day after two down days in a row. In 250 days of one share the pattern occurred 9 times: down followed 6 times and up 3.
screens.question: With add-one smoothing over the two outcomes, what is the chance of down? Give a decimal to 4 places.

hints.text: Add 1 to each of the two counts.

feedback.correct: $7/11 = 0.6364$, pulled a little toward one half.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add 1 to both counts, then normalise.

byKey.mle: That is the unsmoothed share, $6/9$. With 9 cases the share is shaky; smoothing pulls it toward one half.
byKey.one-cell: You added 1 to the total once. Each of the two outcomes gains 1, so the total gains 2.

explain.text: Add-one gives $(6 + 1)/(9 + 2) = 7/11 = 0.6364$. With 9 cases, a pattern never seen would get chance 0 without it. With 900 cases the smoothing would barely move the share.

ideas: A row’s log-likelihood is $\sum_b N_{ab} \ln q_b = -N_a H(\hat p_a, q)$, largest exactly when $q = \hat p_a$: the counts over the row total are the MLE.
Divide each row by its own total. Dividing by the table’s total gives pair chances, and no row then adds to 1.
A zero count makes a new name impossible. Add $\alpha$ to every count; choose it on dev names: 0.1 and 1 tie at 2.4514.

quiz.question: What happens to a row as $\alpha$ grows very large?

options.text: It tends to the counts’ shares
options.why: That is $\alpha \to 0$. A huge $\alpha$ swamps the counts.
Each row still adds to 1, since it is divided by its total.
